deep.reconstruction:
Context: E477 studies Euler's double series, written here as ∫1/z^m (1/y^n) = Σ_{z≥1} z^{-m} Σ_{y≤z} y^{-n}. In modern terms these are non-strict double zeta values ζ★(m,n), and each 'ordo' m+n=λ is a weight. §24 sums up what has been obtained so far.

(i) The first method gives the symmetric case. With m+n=2μ: ζ★(μ,μ) = ½ζ(μ)² + ½ζ(2μ). This is the stuffle (harmonic product) relation ζ(μ)² = 2ζ★(μ,μ) − ζ(2μ) for the diagonal.

(ii) The second method gives one further evaluable series in every weight. This is the formula on the previous page: 2ζ★(λ−1,1) = (λ+1)ζ(λ) − Σ_{k=2}^{λ−2} ζ(k)ζ(λ−k).

(iii) With these and the general relations, in weight 6 every double series can be summed, i.e. reduced to ζ(6), ζ(3)² and similar products. Euler suspects ('suspicari licet') that this works in every weight, even though the second method alone does not finish the job.

(iv) He stresses a key point. If in each weight one further series, besides the two already mentioned, could be summed by any means, all the others would follow. That holds in the weights treated so far, but going further 'more than one determination is found to be lacking'. He thus retracts the conjecture: the linear system leaves a rank deficit greater than one at higher weight.

Section 25 starts a compact notation to make the linear systems transparent, for weight λ:
- p^μ (= p^ν, with μ+ν=λ) denotes the product ζ(μ)ζ(ν), not a power;
- p^λ denotes ζ(λ);
- q^μ (next page) denotes ζ★(μ, λ−μ).

The next page then tabulates, weight by weight, the equations from the first method (stuffle: q^μ + q^ν = p^μ + p^λ) and from the second method (sums with binomial-type coefficients, a shuffle/partial-fraction type relation). This is effectively Euler's double-shuffle linear algebra for double zeta values.
errors: No mathematical error on this page. The symmetric formula is correct for Euler's non-strict convention (y≤z).

Euler's closing claim that more than one determination is lacking at higher weights may reflect the incompleteness of his own system rather than the true count. In modern terms, full double shuffle relations leave exactly one undetermined double zeta in weight 8 (e.g. ζ(5,3) modulo products). The deficit grows only slowly with weight, roughly floor((w−2)/6) in even weight (Gangl–Kaneko–Zagier). The page does not say which weight he examined, so this cannot be checked from the page alone.

ideas.modern_name: stuffle/harmonic product relation for the diagonal double zeta

ideas.what: Conjecture that all double series of every weight reduce to products of single zeta values, followed by the observation that beyond the computed weights the linear system leaves more than one unknown undetermined
ideas.modern_name: reducibility of double zeta values; irreducible double zetas from weight 8 (e.g. ζ(5,3)); dimension of double zeta space modulo products
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler for the question. Modern resolution/conjectures by Borwein–Bradley–Broadhurst, Zagier, and Gangl–Kaneko–Zagier (2006), linking the deficit to cusp forms / period polynomials

ideas.what: Compact notation p^μ, q^μ for the linear system of each weight (double-shuffle style bookkeeping)
ideas.modern_name: linear algebra of double shuffle relations

missed.claim: Euler explicitly notices a rank deficit greater than one in his weight-by-weight linear systems beyond weight 6. This is the phenomenon later explained by Gangl–Kaneko–Zagier via cusp forms. Euler's observation of a growing deficit is an early empirical sighting of it. It is generally acknowledged in historical surveys of multiple zeta values, though perhaps not his precise remark about 'plures una'.
missed.quote: at si vlterius progrediamus, plures vna determinationes deficere deprehenduntur
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is of historical interest only. Comparing Euler's (possibly incomplete) relation set with full double shuffle could show which relations he lacked. The mathematics itself is well understood.

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's well-known double zeta paper. The conjecture and its retraction are part of the standard MZV history; at most a minor detail about the size of the deficit is noteworthy.
transcription_corrections: In §25 the printed formula reads '∫1/z^μ · 1/z^ν' (the second ∫ is apparently omitted in the print). It means the product ∫1/z^μ · ∫1/z^ν = ζ(μ)ζ(ν).
'p^μ' and 'p^ν' are superscript labels, not powers.
The order in §24 is 'm+n=6' (printed glyph looks like a 6).
